children: The $22 bln Tata Steel is effectively taking over $5 bln APL Apollo, its finished-products rival. The strategic logic is sound but the price is high and the convoluted structure skews the benefits to the target's chair. That makes it deeply unfair to minority shareholders.
Full view will be published shortly.
Follow Ujjaini Dutta on LinkedIn and X.
Tata Steel on November 22 and November 23 announced two separate deals that could leave it in effective control of rival APL Apollo Tubes, the country's largest structural steel tube maker.

Tata Steel will sell its downstream businesses for finished products including its tubes division to APL Apollo for up to 280 billion Indian rupees ($3.01 billion) in cash. Separately, it agreed to acquire a 26.6% stake in APL Apollo for 155.1 billion rupees ($1.7 billion) from its Chair Sanjay Gupta. APL Apollo shareholders will need to approve the purchase of the Tata units. However, the two deals are not contingent on each other.

The stake purchase will trigger a mandatory offer by Tata Steel on the open market for a further 26% stake in the tube maker. Tata Steel will pay Gupta 2,100 rupees per share and, in the mandatory offer, is offering minority shareholders 2,301 rupees per share.

The deal also includes a signed memorandum of understanding between APL Apollo and SG Tech Engineering, a private company related to Sanjay Gupta, for contract manufacturing facilities of five million metric tons per annum of colour-coated products.
Shares of Tata Steel closed 8.4% down at 163 rupees on November 23 and APL Apollo's closed at 1,670 rupees, down 21% from the previous close.
